### Issue Details

# My use-case
I'm running a local ACME server on my home network (via Caddy's acme_server) on a different machine. I'm using a combination of Caddy and acme.sh to automatically renew certs for TrueNAS, since the TrueNAS GUI seemingly doesn't like being fully proxied for various automation tasks. So my setup is as follows:
- Caddy only on port 80, webroots /.well-known/acme-challenge from disk while proxying everything else to localhost:81
- TrueNAS Web GUI HTTP is listening on port 81
- TrueNAS Web GUI HTTPS is listening on port 443, bypassing Caddy entirely
- acme.sh runs periodically to do a renew, using the webroot for challenges and then running its TrueNAS hook to actually install the certificates into TrueNAS

# The problem
Caddy is simply eating the accesses to /.well-known/acme-challenge/ and not serving them from disk where acme.sh writes them, so renewals were failing.

# Observed behavior (and why this took me quite a few hours to debug)
ACME server was refusing with rejectedIdentifier "The server will not issue certificates for the identifier" - sent me on quite the debugging chain on the ACME server side, but it makes sense it would do that because the TrueNAS Caddy was saying there are no identifiers in the challenges since it wasn't presenting them from the webroot.

And the part that made me realize it - tls and NOP errors in the caddy output:
```
2026/10/01 11:04:28.961 WARN    tls     looking up info for HTTP challenge      {"uri": "/.well-known/acme-challenge/KSXepMFs33ODvWFQK4Sbf1hNokTCHFnr", "identifier": "truenas.nmz", "remote_addr": "192.168.13.6:40764", "user_agent": "Go-http-client/1.1", "error": "no information found to solve challenge for identifier: truenas.nmz"}
2026/10/01 11:04:28.961 INFO    http.log.access NOP     {"request": {"remote_ip": "192.168.13.6", "remote_port": "40764", "client_ip": "192.168.13.6", "proto": "HTTP/1.1", "method": "GET", "host": "truenas.nmz", "uri": "/.well-known/acme-challenge/KSXepMFs33ODvWFQK4Sbf1hNokTCHFnr", "headers": {"User-Agent": ["Go-http-client/1.1"], "Accept-Encoding": ["gzip"]}}, "bytes_read": 0, "user_id": "", "duration": 0.00014009, "size": 0, "status": 0, "resp_headers": {"Server": ["Caddy"]}}
2026/10/01 11:04:29.236 WARN    tls     looking up info for HTTP challenge      {"uri": "/.well-known/acme-challenge/KSXepMFs33ODvWFQK4Sbf1hNokTCHFnr", "identifier": "truenas.nmz", "remote_addr": "192.168.13.15:35610", "user_agent": "acme.sh/3.1.4 (https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh)", "error": "no information found to solve challenge for identifier: truenas.nmz"}
2026/10/01 11:04:29.236 INFO    http.log.access NOP     {"request": {"remote_ip": "192.168.13.15", "remote_port": "35610", "client_ip": "192.168.13.15", "proto": "HTTP/1.1", "method": "GET", "host": "truenas.nmz", "uri": "/.well-known/acme-challenge/KSXepMFs33ODvWFQK4Sbf1hNokTCHFnr", "headers": {"Accept": ["/"], "User-Agent": ["acme.sh/3.1.4 ([https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh)"]}}](https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh)%22]%7D%7D), "bytes_read": 0, "user_id": "", "duration": 0.000256622, "size": 0, "status": 0, "resp_headers": {"Server": ["Caddy"]}}
```
Which is also expected with the prior knowledge of Caddy intercepting the challenges, but was quite frustrating since it meant nothing was showing up in the access log since nothing was ever reaching the webroot handler.

# Versions and configs

Caddy v2.11.4 h1:XKxkMTgNSizEvKG6QHue6cAsFOteU2qA61w2tKkCWi0=
Caddyfile
```
{
    admin off
    auto_https off
}

http://192.168.13.13 {
    bind 192.168.13.13
    handle_path /.well-known/acme-challenge/* {
        root * /mnt/truenas-main/caddy/acme-root/.well-known/acme-challenge
        file_server
    }
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:81
}
```

# What I'd like to see

Actually the exact same thing as 10 years ago with https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/1019, but I'm not sure whether being able to proxy/disable the acme-challenge catcher in Caddy is something desirable by the maintainers, I'm not really of an opinion here - yes it would make my life easier since Caddy is extremely easy to deploy and configure, but there are other solutions to get around this, nowadays rather niche I'd hope, limitation (nginx self-contained in a folder is also relatively simple to set up).

I'm not sure if this issue re-appearing after a decade since the last report is an accidental oversight during one of the numerous Caddy upgrades (v1 -> v2? etc) or whether it was intentional. Though in the latter case I would highly appreciate some sort of warning or something at startup (or just crash outright) when a challenge folder route/proxy is detected, or some big warning about it in the docs - I will admit I have not read every word from the docs but I've seen quite a lot of it and I was not aware of the limitation. If this was accidentally re-introduced, then of course I will welcome a fix - and if I had more than "exactly no idea" about the Caddy codebase I'd probably try to contribute it, but this is just not my field of expertise, sorry.

Thank you for taking the time to look at this issue btw, Caddy is a truly amazing project!

### Assistance Disclosure

AI used

### If AI was used, describe the extent to which it was used.

During the debugging process to bounce ideas off of and analyze logs, since I'm not technical enough in ACME challenge flows, final issue is fully human written.

# My use-case

body_text:
### Issue Details

### Summary

During a configuration reload, the HTTP app can return from `Stop()` while its old servers are still draining active requests. Configuration unload then cancels the old Caddy context and invokes module `Cleanup()` before those requests have finished.

A handler can therefore continue executing after its module has been cleaned up. Resources released by that module are no longer guaranteed to remain usable.

This also reproduces with an unlimited grace period, so it is distinct from the prematurely canceled grace-period timer reported in #8078.

### Relationship to existing work

Related to #8078 and #8082.

The module-lifetime problem is already identified in the review of #8082:
https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/pull/8082#discussion_r4153380035

The subsequent review requests a core cleanup-hold mechanism with an explicit lifecycle contract:
https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/pull/8082#discussion_r4154077493

This issue tracks that underlying module-lifetime problem separately.

### Reproduction

Reproduced against unmodified upstream commit:
`f7eeb1d65c80b2f634b3ce406fa71ba1f0e078a2`

Environment: Linux Docker container, Go 1.26, race detector enabled.

Save the attached `caddy-cleanup-reproduction.go.txt` as
`modules/caddyhttp/app_shutdown_test.go` in that upstream checkout.

Run:

```sh
GOFLAGS='-tags=nobadger,nomysql,nopgx -mod=readonly' \
  go test -race -short ./modules/caddyhttp \
  -run '^TestReloadRetainsActiveHandlerModules$' \
  -count=1 -timeout=30s
```

The test:

1. Loads an instrumented HTTP handler whose `Cleanup()` records when cleanup happens.
2. Starts a request, flushes the beginning of its response, and blocks the handler.
3. Reloads the configuration using `caddy.Load()` while the handler remains blocked.
4. Checks whether module cleanup has already run.
5. Releases the handler and checks response completion and final cleanup.

It covers HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 with an unlimited grace period.

### Actual result

Both protocol cases fail:

```text
--- FAIL: TestReloadRetainsActiveHandlerModules
    --- FAIL: TestReloadRetainsActiveHandlerModules/http2=false
        module cleaned up while its handler was active
    --- FAIL: TestReloadRetainsActiveHandlerModules/http2=true
        module cleaned up while its handler was active
```

### Expected result

Reload may return while the retired servers drain, but module cleanup must wait until the active handler executions and required finalization have finished.

A grace-period deadline may close remaining network connections, but it must not authorize releasing module resources while a handler is still executing.

### Proposed approach

Separate context cancellation from resource cleanup.

An experimental cleanup hold allows the HTTP app to retain its modules during asynchronous shutdown. Cancellation and its cause remain immediate; cleanup runs after the outstanding holders release their holds.

The mechanism needs multiple independent holders, idempotent release, failure-path handling, and bounded process-exit waiting.

An independent implementation and regression tests are available in:
https://github.com/RentnerKev/caddy/compare/8ad83ebd4316d47fa40d11181eef148f018ec159...5cd933bb2863170789f758c7ab20264fe64306fc

### Scope

This report concerns premature module cleanup. It does not claim that all reload-related connection resets or idle HTTP/1 keepalive reuse problems are resolved.

### Assistance Disclosure

AI used

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigating this bug, developing and running reproduction tests.

### Issue Details


Since #7945 (first released in v2.11.5), `Server.ServeHTTP` flushes the response in a deferred func when an HTTP/1.x request that is being access-logged took at least `write_timeout`. If the handler hijacked the connection, e.g. `reverse_proxy` passing through a `101 Switching Protocols` upgrade, that flush panics with a nil pointer dereference.

Reproduced on v2.11.6 and v2.11.7, stock build without plugins.

### Reproduce

`Caddyfile`:

```caddyfile
{
	admin off
	servers {
		timeouts {
			write 1s
		}
	}
}

:8080 {
	log
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:9000
}
```

`upstream.py`: answers every request with 101 and holds the connection until the peer closes it.

```python
import socket, threading

def serve(c):
    c.recv(65536)
    c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\nUpgrade: test\r\n\r\n")
    while c.recv(65536):
        pass
    c.close()

s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000))
s.listen()
while True:
    threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(s.accept()[0],), daemon=True).start()
```

```sh
python3 upstream.py &
caddy run --config Caddyfile &
# keep the upgraded connection open longer than write_timeout
(printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\nUpgrade: test\r\n\r\n'; sleep 2) | nc 127.0.0.1 8080
```

The client gets the 101 and the tunnel works. When it closes, the access log entry is written as usual (`"status":101`, `"duration"` ≈ 2s), and then:

```
{"level":"error","logger":"http.stdlib","msg":"http: panic serving 127.0.0.1:56866: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
goroutine 68 [running]:
net/http.(*conn).serve.func1()
	net/http/server.go:1907 +0xac
panic({0x107588320?, 0x107af6170?})
	runtime/panic.go:860 +0x12c
bufio.(*Writer).Flush(0x1078443d8?)
	bufio/bufio.go:636 +0x18
net/http.(*response).FlushError(0x637fdd514000)
	net/http/server.go:1728 +0x38
net/http.(*ResponseController).Flush(0x637fdd1f6460?)
	net/http/responsecontroller.go:52 +0xdc
github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp.(*IdleTimeoutWriter).FlushError(0x637fdd1f6460)
	github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2@v2.11.7/modules/caddyhttp/idletimeout.go:326 +0x38
net/http.(*ResponseController).Flush(0x1421bcc2e?)
	net/http/responsecontroller.go:52 +0xdc
github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp.(*responseRecorder).FlushError(0x107b21d40?)
	github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2@v2.11.7/modules/caddyhttp/responsewriter.go:244 +0x38
net/http.(*ResponseController).Flush(0x107b03ea0?)
	net/http/responsecontroller.go:52 +0xdc
github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp.(*Server).ServeHTTP.func1()
	github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2@v2.11.7/modules/caddyhttp/server.go:692 +0x88
github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp.(*Server).ServeHTTP(0x637fdd1b6408, {0x10796f7a0, 0x637fdd514000}, 0x637fdd508500)
	github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2@v2.11.7/modules/caddyhttp/server.go:711 +0xfc8
net/http.serverHandler.ServeHTTP({0x637fdd1ba8c0?}, {0x10796f7a0?, 0x637fdd514000?}, 0x1?)
	net/http/server.go:3311 +0xb0
net/http.(*conn).serve(0x637fdd3be630, {0x10797b9d0, 0x637fdd228150})
	net/http/server.go:2073 +0x51c
created by net/http.(*Server).Serve in goroutine 99
	net/http/server.go:3464 +0x37c
```

With `sleep 0.2` (shorter than `write_timeout`) there is no panic, and neither is there for a plain long-running request without the upgrade.

### Cause

The deferred func calls `http.NewResponseController(wrec).Flush()` and ignores `http.ErrHijacked`, which assumes Flush reports a hijacked response that way. It doesn't: `(*response).Hijack` releases the bufio writer and sets `w.w = nil`, and `(*response).FlushError` calls `w.w.Flush()` without checking for a hijack. Only `Write` and `WriteHeader` check `hijacked()` and return `ErrHijacked`.

### Impact

net/http recovers the panic, and it fires only after the upgraded stream has ended, so clients don't notice. But every upgraded connection that lives longer than `write_timeout` ends with an error-level stack trace. We hit this in production with headscale behind `reverse_proxy` (`/ts2021` control protocol and `/derp`, both HTTP/1.1 upgrades) and `write 30s`, so practically every client session produces one.

### Possible fix

Let `responseRecorder` remember the hijack and report it from `FlushError`; the deferred func already skips `http.ErrHijacked`:

```diff
--- a/modules/caddyhttp/responsewriter.go
+++ b/modules/caddyhttp/responsewriter.go
@@ -70,6 +70,7 @@ type responseRecorder struct {
 	size         int
 	wroteHeader  bool
 	stream       bool
+	hijacked     bool
 
 	readSize *int
 }
@@ -239,6 +240,11 @@ func (rr *responseRecorder) WriteResponse() error {
 // FlushError will suppress actual flushing if the response is buffered. See:
 // https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/6144
 func (rr *responseRecorder) FlushError() error {
+	// after a hijack the underlying writer is gone; net/http's FlushError
+	// doesn't check for that and dereferences a nil bufio.Writer
+	if rr.hijacked {
+		return http.ErrHijacked
+	}
 	if rr.stream {
 		//nolint:bodyclose
 		return http.NewResponseController(rr.ResponseWriterWrapper).Flush()
@@ -258,6 +264,7 @@ func (rr *responseRecorder) Hijack() (net.Conn, *bufio.ReadWriter, error) {
 	if err != nil {
 		return nil, nil, err
 	}
+	rr.hijacked = true
 	// Per http documentation, returned bufio.Writer is empty, but bufio.Read maybe not
 	conn = &hijackedConn{conn, rr}
 	brw.Writer.Reset(conn)
```

With this patch on v2.11.7 the reproduction no longer panics, the access log entry stays the same (`"status":101`, no error), and `go test ./modules/caddyhttp/ ./modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/` passes. Happy to open a PR with a regression test.

### Summary

On some client paths (T-Mobile USA fixed-wireless home internet here), quic-go's path MTU discovery settles a few bytes above what the path delivers, and HTTP/3 to Caddy then slows 10 to 25x or stalls. Caddy hard-codes the QUIC config (`listeners.go`), so there is no way to cap the QUIC packet size or turn off PMTUD short of patching Caddy. Could Caddy expose that, for example a `quic { max_packet_size 1350 }` (or `disable_pmtud`) option under the global `servers` block?

### Environment

- Caddy 2.11.4 (quic-go v0.59.1), Ubuntu 24.04 VPS, default HTTP/3 settings
- Client: Chrome 151 (Linux and Windows), T-Mobile USA (AS21928)

### What I measured

Raw UDP from the server to the client with DF set: payloads up to 1432 bytes (1460-byte IP packets) are 100% delivered; 1436 bytes and up are 0% delivered, and no ICMP "fragmentation needed" comes back.

quic-go's DPLPMTUD sometimes gets its 1441-byte probe acknowledged and then sends every full-size packet at 1441 bytes. Server-side qlog over 22 fresh connections, 5 MB downloads each:

| final MTU | throughput | losses (all spurious) |
|---|---|---|
| 1366 to 1430 | 21 to 60 Mbit/s | 0 to 3 |
| 1441 | 2.3 to 6.1 Mbit/s | 54 to 269 |

Stock Caddy collapsed this way in 5 to 6 of every 10 fresh connections. HTTP/2 to the same Caddy, and HTTP/3 to dl.google.com (which caps near 1350 bytes), ran at 50 to 85 Mbit/s over the same link.

The same Caddy 2.11.4, patched to set `DisablePathMTUDiscovery: true` and `InitialPacketSize: 1350` on the `quic.Config` passed to `ListenEarly`, never collapsed: 10 of 10 connections stayed under the limit, 9 of 10 with zero losses.

When oversized packets stop arriving entirely after discovery has finished (simulated by dropping outgoing UDP over 1460 bytes on the server), a 400 KB fetch hung 21.6 s until Chrome closed the session ("Network blackhole detected", QUIC error 85). With the 1350-byte build: 0.3 s.

### Related

- #7885 (initial packet size vs a 1280-byte MTU on Tailscale) is the same family: Caddy users currently cannot tune quic-go's packet size settings at all.
- The missing black-hole detection after PMTUD is filed with quic-go: https://github.com/quic-go/quic-go/issues/5914

For now we send `Alt-Svc: clear` on our sites, which works but gives up HTTP/3 for everyone. A config option would let us keep it with a 1350-byte cap.

body_text:
### Issue Details

Hello, I ran into issues with caddy when I was torture testing a rust webdav server i've been developing. I was seeing unexplained 'request header fields too large' errors when using caddy as a reverse tls proxy, and had an agent help debug it and write a patch. What follows now is the agent's writeup, and the patch it wrote. The attached patch (and a related patch for go's net/http/transport.go) fixed the issue for me.

## 1. What version of Caddy are you using?

v2.11.7 (commit `72dd0fb067f6d7826c7f79907670ba4a713bfe37`), built with Go 1.26.
Reproduced identically on the stock `caddy:v2.11.7` binary.

## 2. What are you trying to do?

Proxy a WebDAV-style workload where the upstream legitimately answers a request
**before** the client has finished uploading the body (e.g. `423 Locked`,
`411`/`413`/`401` returned from headers alone, then the upstream closes the
connection without draining the body). After relaying that early response, the
client connection should be safe to reuse or close cleanly.

## 3. What is the problem and what does it look like?

When the upstream responds early and closes while the client is still sending
the body, Caddy relays the response correctly **but leaves the client
connection open without draining the remaining request-body bytes**. The next
request pipelined on that same connection then has its leftover body bytes
parsed as header lines, and Go's HTTP parser answers:

```
HTTP/1.1 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
```

This 431 is generated by `net/http`'s server parser *below* Caddy's handler
chain, so it is **not logged by Caddy at all** and the second request never
reaches the upstream. The connection is silently corrupted for the client.

This violates RFC 9110 §6.5: after responding, a server must either drain the
remaining request body or close the connection — it must not leave unread body
bytes on a connection it keeps open.

## 4. What is the exact error message you saw (if any)?

No Caddy log entry. The client sees `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` on
the *second* request; the upstream log shows the second request never arrived.

## 5. What did you expect to happen?

Either:
- Caddy drains the leftover request body (up to the usual limit) and reuses the
  connection cleanly, **or**
- Caddy closes the client connection after relaying the early response, so the
  client retries the next request on a fresh connection.

## 6. What happened instead?

Caddy neither drained nor closed: the connection stayed open with unread body
bytes, and the next pipelined request was mis-parsed as oversized headers (431).

## 7. How can we reproduce it?

Three pieces, all on one host.

**Upstream** (`up.py`) — answers `/early` with `423` + `Connection: close`
*without reading the request body*, then closes (emulates a WebDAV lock-null /
early-error backend):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, sys, threading

def handle(c):
    buf = b""
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in buf:
        d = c.recv(4096)
        if not d:
            return
        buf += d
    head = buf.split(b"\r\n\r\n")[0].decode("latin1")
    path = head.split("\r\n")[0].split(" ")[1]
    print(f"REQ {head.splitlines()[0]!r}", flush=True)
    if path == "/early":
        # Respond WITHOUT reading the body, then close.
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 423 Locked\r\nContent-Length: 8\r\n"
                  b"Connection: close\r\n\r\n<D:error")
    else:
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nok")
    c.close()

ln = socket.socket(); ln.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
ln.bind(("127.0.0.1", 18999)); ln.listen(64)
while True:
    c, _ = ln.accept(); threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(c,)).start()
```

**Caddyfile** (`Caddyfile`):

```
{
	admin off
	auto_https disable_redirects
}
http://127.0.0.1:8444 {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:18999
}
```

**Client** (`cl.py`) — sends `PUT /early` with a 200 KB body, dribbles it
(8 KiB / 20 ms) *after* reading the early 423, then pipelines `GET /second` on
the **same** connection (exactly what a pooled HTTP client does):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, time
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8444))
s.sendall(b"PUT /early HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:8444\r\nContent-Length: 200000\r\n\r\n")
s.sendall(b"A" * 1000)
resp = b""
while b"\r\n\r\n" not in resp:
    resp += s.recv(4096)
print("resp1:", resp.split(b"\r\n")[0])          # -> 423 (correct)
while len(resp) < len(resp.split(b"\r\n\r\n")[0]) + 4 + 8:
    resp += s.recv(4096)                          # consume the 423's 8-byte body
sent = 1000
try:
    while sent < 200000:                          # keep dribbling the body
        n = min(8192, 200000 - sent)
        s.sendall(b"B" * n); sent += n; time.sleep(0.02)
except OSError as e:
    print("body write failed:", e)
s.sendall(b"GET /second HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:8444\r\nConnection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n")
s.settimeout(5)
r2 = b""
try:
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in r2:
        d = s.recv(4096)
        if not d: break
        r2 += d
except socket.timeout:
    pass
print("resp2:", (r2.split(b"\r\n")[0] if r2 else b"<closed>"))
```

Run: `python3 up.py &` → `caddy run --config Caddyfile` → `python3 cl.py`.

### Control (no Caddy): point the client at the upstream directly (port 18999)

```
resp1: b'HTTP/1.1 423 Locked'
body write failed: [Errno 32] Broken pipe
resp2: b''            # connection closed — correct per RFC 9110 §6.5
```

### Test (through Caddy, port 8444):

```
resp1: b'HTTP/1.1 423 Locked'
resp2: b'HTTP/1.1 431 Request Header Fields Too Large'   # BUG
```

The upstream log confirms `GET /second` never reached it.

## 8. Why it happens (source pointers)

Caddy wraps the request body in `bodyNopCloserIfNotRead`
(`modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/reverseproxy.go:569`) and streams the response
in `finalizeResponse`/`copyResponse`. After the handler returns, `net/http`'s
`(*conn).finishRequest` tries to drain the unconsumed request body
(`server.go`, the `maxPostHandlerReadBytes` path) — but the transport's
`writeLoop` still holds the body mutex while blocked reading the (slow) client
body. The drain neither completes nor forces a close, so the connection is
reused with leftover body bytes still on the wire.

A `pprof /debug/pprof/goroutine` dump taken mid-dribble shows the handler
goroutine already gone (423 delivered) and the connection goroutine parked in
`finishRequest` → `chunkWriter.writeHeader` → `body.Read` (the post-handler
drain), while the transport `writeLoop` is blocked in `ReadFrom` on the same
body.

## 9. Proposed fix

In `finalizeResponse`, when the upstream answered before the client finished
sending the body (HTTP/1, `ContentLength >= 0`, and the body wrapper's
bytes-read < `ContentLength`), set `Connection: close` on the response. That
makes `net/http` skip the racy drain and close the connection instead of
reusing it desynced. (The body-read counter also needs to be atomic, since the
transport's body copy reads it concurrently.)

Verified: with this change the client sees the 423 and a clean connection close
instead of 431, across 30/30 runs; the control path (small complete body) is
unchanged. Patch attached.

## 10. Related

{"repository": "caddyserver/caddy", "task_candidate_id": 2688, "repository_id": 51, "issue_number": 8196, "github_issue_id": 5801048661, "html_url": "https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/8196", "created_at": "2026-10-11T12:28:39+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "Go 1.26 can desynchronise HTTP/1 connections after early upstream responses", "body_text": "### Issue Details

Hello, I ran into issues with caddy when I was torture testing a rust webdav server i've been developing. I was seeing unexplained 'request header fields too large' errors when using caddy as a reverse tls proxy, and had an agent help debug it and write a patch. What follows now is the agent's writeup, and the patch it wrote. The attached patch (and a related patch for go's net/http/transport.go) fixed the issue for me.

## 1. What version of Caddy are you using?

v2.11.7 (commit `72dd0fb067f6d7826c7f79907670ba4a713bfe37`), built with Go 1.26.
Reproduced identically on the stock `caddy:v2.11.7` binary.

## 2. What are you trying to do?

Proxy a WebDAV-style workload where the upstream legitimately answers a request
**before** the client has finished uploading the body (e.g. `423 Locked`,
`411`/`413`/`401` returned from headers alone, then the upstream closes the
connection without draining the body). After relaying that early response, the
client connection should be safe to reuse or close cleanly.

## 3. What is the problem and what does it look like?

When the upstream responds early and closes while the client is still sending
the body, Caddy relays the response correctly **but leaves the client
connection open without draining the remaining request-body bytes**. The next
request pipelined on that same connection then has its leftover body bytes
parsed as header lines, and Go's HTTP parser answers:

```
HTTP/1.1 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
```

This 431 is generated by `net/http`'s server parser *below* Caddy's handler
chain, so it is **not logged by Caddy at all** and the second request never
reaches the upstream. The connection is silently corrupted for the client.

This violates RFC 9110 §6.5: after responding, a server must either drain the
remaining request body or close the connection — it must not leave unread body
bytes on a connection it keeps open.

## 4. What is the exact error message you saw (if any)?

No Caddy log entry. The client sees `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` on
the *second* request; the upstream log shows the second request never arrived.

## 5. What did you expect to happen?

Either:
- Caddy drains the leftover request body (up to the usual limit) and reuses the
  connection cleanly, **or**
- Caddy closes the client connection after relaying the early response, so the
  client retries the next request on a fresh connection.

## 6. What happened instead?

Caddy neither drained nor closed: the connection stayed open with unread body
bytes, and the next pipelined request was mis-parsed as oversized headers (431).

## 7. How can we reproduce it?

Three pieces, all on one host.

**Upstream** (`up.py`) — answers `/early` with `423` + `Connection: close`
*without reading the request body*, then closes (emulates a WebDAV lock-null /
early-error backend):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, sys, threading

def handle(c):
    buf = b""
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in buf:
        d = c.recv(4096)
        if not d:
            return
        buf += d
    head = buf.split(b"\r\n\r\n")[0].decode("latin1")
    path = head.split("\r\n")[0].split(" ")[1]
    print(f"REQ {head.splitlines()[0]!r}", flush=True)
    if path == "/early":
        # Respond WITHOUT reading the body, then close.
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 423 Locked\r\nContent-Length: 8\r\n"
                  b"Connection: close\r\n\r\n<D:error")
    else:
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nok")
    c.close()

ln = socket.socket(); ln.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
ln.bind(("127.0.0.1", 18999)); ln.listen(64)
while True:
    c, _ = ln.accept(); threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(c,)).start()
```

**Caddyfile** (`Caddyfile`):

```
{
	admin off
	auto_https disable_redirects
}
http://127.0.0.1:8444 {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:18999
}
```

**Client** (`cl.py`) — sends `PUT /early` with a 200 KB body, dribbles it
(8 KiB / 20 ms) *after* reading the early 423, then pipelines `GET /second` on
the **same** connection (exactly what a pooled HTTP client does):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, time
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8444))
s.sendall(b"PUT /early HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:8444\r\nContent-Length: 200000\r\n\r\n")
s.sendall(b"A" * 1000)
resp = b""
while b"\r\n\r\n" not in resp:
    resp += s.recv(4096)
print("resp1:", resp.split(b"\r\n")[0])          # -> 423 (correct)
while len(resp) < len(resp.split(b"\r\n\r\n")[0]) + 4 + 8:
    resp += s.recv(4096)                          # consume the 423's 8-byte body
sent = 1000
try:
    while sent < 200000:                          # keep dribbling the body
        n = min(8192, 200000 - sent)
        s.sendall(b"B" * n); sent += n; time.sleep(0.02)
except OSError as e:
    print("body write failed:", e)
s.sendall(b"GET /second HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:8444\r\nConnection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n")
s.settimeout(5)
r2 = b""
try:
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in r2:
        d = s.recv(4096)
        if not d: break
        r2 += d
except socket.timeout:
    pass
print("resp2:", (r2.split(b"\r\n")[0] if r2 else b"<closed>"))
```

Run: `python3 up.py &` → `caddy run --config Caddyfile` → `python3 cl.py`.

### Control (no Caddy): point the client at the upstream directly (port 18999)

```
resp1: b'HTTP/1.1 423 Locked'
body write failed: [Errno 32] Broken pipe
resp2: b''            # connection closed — correct per RFC 9110 §6.5
```

### Test (through Caddy, port 8444):

```
resp1: b'HTTP/1.1 423 Locked'
resp2: b'HTTP/1.1 431 Request Header Fields Too Large'   # BUG
```

The upstream log confirms `GET /second` never reached it.

## 8. Why it happens (source pointers)

Caddy wraps the request body in `bodyNopCloserIfNotRead`
(`modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/reverseproxy.go:569`) and streams the response
in `finalizeResponse`/`copyResponse`. After the handler returns, `net/http`'s
`(*conn).finishRequest` tries to drain the unconsumed request body
(`server.go`, the `maxPostHandlerReadBytes` path) — but the transport's
`writeLoop` still holds the body mutex while blocked reading the (slow) client
body. The drain neither completes nor forces a close, so the connection is
reused with leftover body bytes still on the wire.

A `pprof /debug/pprof/goroutine` dump taken mid-dribble shows the handler
goroutine already gone (423 delivered) and the connection goroutine parked in
`finishRequest` → `chunkWriter.writeHeader` → `body.Read` (the post-handler
drain), while the transport `writeLoop` is blocked in `ReadFrom` on the same
body.

## 9. Proposed fix

In `finalizeResponse`, when the upstream answered before the client finished
sending the body (HTTP/1, `ContentLength >= 0`, and the body wrapper's
bytes-read < `ContentLength`), set `Connection: close` on the response. That
makes `net/http` skip the racy drain and close the connection instead of
reusing it desynced. (The body-read counter also needs to be atomic, since the
transport's body copy reads it concurrently.)

Verified: with this change the client sees the 423 and a clean connection close
instead of 431, across 30/30 runs; the control path (small complete body) is
unchanged. Patch attached.

### Issue Details

Active health checks with `follow_redirects: true` use the redirect’s Host header but still connect to the original backend.

Reproduced on Linux.

### Reproduction

Run two HTTP backends on the same machine:

- **Backend A, port 19001:** `/health` returns a 302 redirect to `http://127.0.0.1:19002/ready`. Its own `/ready` returns 503.
- **Backend B, port 19002:** `/ready` returns 200.

Configure Caddy to proxy to A, with active health checks using `/health` and `follow_redirects: true`.

**Expected:** Caddy follows the redirect to B, receives 200, and keeps A available.

**Actual:** Caddy sends the redirected `/ready` request to A’s port, despite setting `Host: 127.0.0.1:19002`. It receives 503, marks A unhealthy, and proxied requests return `503 no upstreams available`.

For comparison, `curl -i -L http://127.0.0.1:19001/health` correctly reaches B and returns 200.

### Cause and scope
Redirects inherit the original `DialInfo`, which `HTTPTransport` continues using. This can produce false healthy or unhealthy results. Redirect following must be enabled; same-origin redirects work.

body_text:
### Issue Details

reverse_proxy drops the values of request trailers. The upstream sees the
trailer key but no value after reading the body to EOF. Same with HTTP/1.1 and
HTTP/2 clients, and with TCP and unix socket upstreams. Sending the value as a
header instead works.

Caddy v2.11.7 (`caddy:2` image), upstream and client built with Go 1.25.6.

Repro, all three in the same network namespace:

Caddyfile:

```
{
	admin off
}

http://:8080 {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:7100
}
```

Upstream:

```go
package main

import (
	"io"
	"log"
	"net/http"
)

func main() {
	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:7100", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		io.Copy(io.Discard, r.Body)
		log.Printf("trailer=%q", r.Trailer)
	})))
}
```

Client:

```go
package main

import (
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	req, _ := http.NewRequest("PUT", os.Args[1], io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader("hello")))
	req.ContentLength = -1
	req.Trailer = http.Header{"Content-Digest": {"sha-256=:LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ=:"}}
	resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	resp.Body.Close()
}
```

Upstream log, first direct (`client http://127.0.0.1:7100/`), then through Caddy (`client http://127.0.0.1:8080/`):

```
trailer=map["Content-Digest":["sha-256=:LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ=:"]]
trailer=map["Content-Digest":[]]
```

### Assistance Disclosure

AI used

### If AI was used, describe the extent to which it was used.

This came up during planning of an API where we used Caddy as a prototype frontend to handle TLS termination.

The repro code was 100% designed by AI. This repro was posted with gh cli.

reverse_proxy drops the values of request trailers. The upstream sees the
trailer key but no value after reading the body to EOF. Same with HTTP/1.1 and
HTTP/2 clients, and with TCP and unix socket upstreams. Sending the value as a
header instead works.

Caddy v2.11.7 (`caddy:2` image), upstream and client built with Go 1.25.6.

Repro, all three in the same network namespace:

Caddyfile:

```
{
	admin off
}

http://:8080 {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:7100
}
```

Upstream:

```go
package main

import (
	"io"
	"log"
	"net/http"
)

func main() {
	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:7100", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		io.Copy(io.Discard, r.Body)
		log.Printf("trailer=%q", r.Trailer)
	})))
}
```

Client:

```go
package main

import (
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	req, _ := http.NewRequest("PUT", os.Args[1], io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader("hello")))
	req.ContentLength = -1
	req.Trailer = http.Header{"Content-Digest": {"sha-256=:LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ=:"}}
	resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	resp.Body.Close()
}
```

```
trailer=map["Content-Digest":["sha-256=:LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ=:"]]
trailer=map["Content-Digest":[]]
```

body_text:
### Issue Details

#7832 added a `Provision` step which uppercases every configured method. HTTP method tokens are case-sensitive under [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.1) and Go preserves the casing of extension methods.

For example:
```caddyfile
:8080 {
	@custom method foo
	respond @custom "matched"
	respond "missed"
}
```

```sh
curl -X foo http://localhost:8080
```

The request should return matched but the configured `foo` is changed to `FOO` during provisioning so it returns missed.

Caddyfile and native JSON matchers are provisioned and uppercased while CEL method matchers preserve the configured case. All three configuration paths should preserve and compare the exact method token. Standard methods must be configured with their normal uppercase spelling while case-sensitive extension methods must remain unchanged.

body_text:
### Issue Details

The `query` log filter reads `#` in the logged request URI as the start of a fragment. A request-target has no fragment, so Caddy and the backend treat everything after `#` as part of the query, and a parameter there is logged unredacted:

```
{
	admin off
}
:28480 {
	log {
		output file ./access.log
		format filter {
			request>uri query {
				replace token REDACTED
			}
		}
	}
	respond "ok"
}
```

```
$ printf 'GET /a?x=1#&token=s3cr3t HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 28480
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
$ printf 'GET /a?token=s3cr3t#%%zz HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 28480
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
$ jq -r .request.uri access.log
/a?x=1#&token=s3cr3t
/a?token=s3cr3t#%zz
```

`GET /a?token=s3cr3t` on the same server logs `/a?token=REDACTED`. curl and browsers strip `#...` before sending, so this needs a client that sends a raw `#`.

Version: v2.11.7 (release binary) and master at 719db53e.

Cause: `QueryFilter.processQueryString` in `modules/logging/filters.go` uses `url.Parse`. For `/a?x=1#&token=s3cr3t` it puts `&token=s3cr3t` in the fragment and filters only `x=1`. For `/a?token=s3cr3t#%zz` the fragment has an invalid escape, `url.Parse` fails, and the filter returns the value unchanged. Go's server parses the request line with `url.ParseRequestURI`, which has no fragment, so the backend gets `token=s3cr3t`.

I have a patch with a test that parses values starting with `/` with `url.ParseRequestURI`. Values like absolute Referer or Location URLs keep `url.Parse`. One side effect: a relative `Location: /a?x=1#section` filtered with `query` would now read `#section` as part of the query too. Absolute-form request-targets (`GET http://host/a?...`, forward proxy use) stay as they are.

### Assistance Disclosure

AI used

### If AI was used, describe the extent to which it was used.

AI used (Claude Code).

body_text:
### Description

Caddy v2.11.4 running as a native Windows service intermittently remains stuck in the `START_PENDING` state after a Windows Server VM reboot, despite the Caddy process running successfully and serving HTTP/HTTPS traffic.

The service is configured with **Automatic (Delayed Start)** and runs under a group Managed Service Account (gMSA).

Running `caddy reload` immediately corrects the Windows service status to `RUNNING`, without needing to terminate or restart the Caddy process.

### Environment

- **Caddy version:** `v2.11.4 h1:XKxkMTgNSizEvKG6QHue6cAsFOteU2qA61w2tKkCWi0=`
- **OS:** Windows Server 2022 (Build 20348)
- **Service type:** Native Windows service (`sc.exe`)
- **Startup type:** Automatic (Delayed Start)
- **Service name:** `Caddy`

Service configuration:

```text
SERVICE_NAME: Caddy
        TYPE               : 10  WIN32_OWN_PROCESS
        START_TYPE         : 2   AUTO_START (DELAYED)
        ERROR_CONTROL      : 1   NORMAL
        BINARY_PATH_NAME   : D:\Caddy\caddy.exe run --config D:\Caddy\Caddyfile
        DISPLAY_NAME       : Caddy
        DEPENDENCIES       :
        SERVICE_START_NAME : DOMAIN\gMSA_ServCaddy$
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install Caddy v2.11.4 as a native Windows service using `sc.exe`.
2. Configure the service for Automatic (Delayed Start).
3. Configure the service to run under a gMSA.
4. Reboot the Windows Server VM.
5. Once the VM has started, inspect the service using:

   ```powershell
   sc.exe queryex Caddy
   ```

6. Observe that the service remains in `START_PENDING`, despite Caddy running and successfully serving traffic.
7. Execute:

   ```powershell
   D:\Caddy\caddy.exe reload --config D:\Caddy\Caddyfile
   ```

8. Observe that the Windows service transitions to `RUNNING`.

### Actual behaviour

After reboot, the Windows service reports:

```text
SERVICE_NAME: QpsCaddy
        TYPE               : 10  WIN32_OWN_PROCESS
        STATE              : 2  START_PENDING
                                (NOT_STOPPABLE, NOT_PAUSABLE, IGNORES_SHUTDOWN)
        WIN32_EXIT_CODE    : 0  (0x0)
        SERVICE_EXIT_CODE  : 0  (0x0)
        CHECKPOINT         : 0x0
        WAIT_HINT          : 0x0
        PID                : 10636
        FLAGS              :
```

The Caddy process is running:

```text
ProcessId  CommandLine
--------- -----------
10636      D:\Caddy\caddy.exe run --config D:\Caddy\Caddyfile
```

The process ID matches the PID reported by the Windows Service Control Manager.
HTTP/HTTPS traffic continues to function normally.

Attempting to stop or restart the service through Windows Service Control Manager does not resolve the issue while the service is stuck in `START_PENDING`.

To manually recover without a reload, the Caddy process must first be terminated and the Windows service started again.
However, executing `caddy reload` successfully resolves the service state without restarting the process.

The issue has only been observed following VM reboot.

### Expected behaviour

Following a VM reboot, Caddy should:

1. Start automatically through Windows Service Control Manager.
2. Load its configuration and begin serving traffic.
3. Transition from `START_PENDING` to `RUNNING`.
4. Remain manageable through standard Windows service controls, including stop and restart.

### Possible cause

One possible explanation is a race condition involving native Windows service initialization and Caddy's readiness notification.

If Caddy completes its startup and emits its readiness notification before the Windows service status channel is initialized, the notification may be missed.

This could explain why:

- The Caddy process starts and serves traffic normally.
- Windows continues reporting `START_PENDING`.
- A subsequent `caddy reload` causes Windows to report `RUNNING`.

This is a hypothesis based on the observed behaviour.

### Additional observations

- The issue appears specifically associated with VM reboot.
- Automatic (Delayed Start) is already enabled.
- Windows Service Control Manager reports the correct Caddy process ID.
- Reloading Caddy resolves the incorrect service state.
- The gMSA's involvement has not been established as a contributing factor.
- No Caddy application error logs or Windows event logs have yet been collected to confirm the underlying cause.

### Assistance Disclosure

AI used

### If AI was used, describe the extent to which it was used.

ChatGPT assisted with troubleshooting the Windows service behaviour, interpreting PowerShell and Service Control Manager output, and identifying a possible Windows service readiness race condition.

**Describe the bug**:

A CertificateRequest with `Ready=False`, reason `Failed`, and no `status.failureTime` is never replaced when the private key is reused. The Certificate's `failedIssuanceAttempts` climbs on every retry and the same request stays in place.

`metav1.Time.Before` returns false on a nil receiver, so the request manager's previous-issuance check never fires:

https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/blob/f2cafccba8ef502a08802b720a6deccf67530663/pkg/controller/certificates/requestmanager/requestmanager_controller.go#L284

The issuing controller's matching guard requires `FailureTime != nil`, so it skips and the request reaches `failIssueCertificate` on every issuance:

https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/blob/f2cafccba8ef502a08802b720a6deccf67530663/pkg/controller/certificates/issuing/issuing_controller.go#L305-L306

Found by @wallrj while reviewing #9287, which fixes the mirror case of a `failureTime` with no Ready condition. Raised separately because the fix is not the same one.

**Expected behaviour**:

The request is replaced on the next attempt, the way a `Ready=False/Failed` request with a `failureTime` is.

**Steps to reproduce the bug**:

Set `Ready=False` with reason `Failed` on the CertificateRequest for the current revision and leave `status.failureTime` unset. No in-tree issuer produces this: `Reporter.Failed` sets both fields in one update.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

I ran the trigger, keymanager, request manager and issuing controllers against an envtest apiserver, marked the first request that way, and crossed the retry backoff three times:

| rotationPolicy | failedIssuanceAttempts after 3 retries | same CertificateRequest object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default (`Always`) | 1 | no, replaced on the first retry |
| `Never` | 4 | yes |

With the default policy the keymanager rotates the next private key, the existing spec and key mismatch check removes the request, and the issuance recovers. With a reused key nothing removes it.

Deleting when `failureTime` is nil is not the fix on its own. The request manager can run before the issuing controller and would replace the request before the failure is recorded, which loses the backoff.

**Environment details**:
- Kubernetes version: envtest 1.36.2
- cert-manager version: master (`f2cafccb`)
- Install method: none, the controllers were run directly against envtest

/kind bug

body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
<!--A clear and concise description of what the problem is-->

The cert-manager controller's ServiceAccount often needs access to external DNS infrastructure when using ACME DNS01 challenges.

With workload identity, this can mean granting the cert-manager ServiceAccount permission to modify DNS zones. In a multi-tenant cluster, this can give the controller access to DNS infrastructure unrelated to a particular Issuer.

Several DNS providers already support workload identity, and cert-manager already has a similar mechanism in the Route53 solver.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
<!--A clear and concise description of what you want to happen.-->

Allow a DNS01 solver to specify a ServiceAccount whose identity should be used when accessing the DNS provider:

```yaml
solvers:
- selector:
    dnsZones:
    - example.com
  dns01:
    serviceAccountRef:
      name: dns01
    azureDNS:
      ...
```

cert-manager would use the Kubernetes TokenRequest API to obtain a short-lived **bound ServiceAccount token** for the referenced ServiceAccount. This is the same type of token commonly used as a **projected ServiceAccount token** for workload identity.

The token can then be exchanged with the provider's workload identity mechanism, without granting the cert-manager controller's own ServiceAccount access to the external infrastructure.

The namespace should be implicit:

* For an `Issuer`, the ServiceAccount must be in the Issuer's namespace.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Yes. Currently, when utilizing `dns-01` challenges for an apex domain and a wildcard certificate (e.g., `example.com` and `*.example.com`), there is a strict limitation where the `_acme-challenge` DNS record must point to a single destination. 

In our infrastructure at Example Corp, we utilize a multi-tenant edge architecture where multiple distinct systems need to issue certificates for the same root domain or its subdomains concurrently. Specifically, we have:
1. `cert-manager` managing wildcard certificates in our Kubernetes clusters via AWS Route53 DNS-01 validation.
2. Fastly terminating edge traffic.
3. Kinsta hosting marketing web properties.

Because Fastly and Kinsta both require CNAME delegation for `_acme-challenge.example.com` to their own validation servers, it creates a direct conflict with `cert-manager`'s requirement to inject TXT records at that exact same namespace. We are forced to use brittle workarounds, such as moving edge providers to HTTP-01 or complex CI/CD synchronization pipelines to push clustered certificates outward.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like `cert-manager` to support the new `dns-account-01` challenge type. 

By incorporating a hash of the ACME Account URL into the DNS label (e.g., `_acme-challenge_accountUniqueValue.example.com`), `cert-manager` could request and validate certificates using a unique namespace that does not clash with the standard `_acme-challenge` CNAME delegations required by our external CDNs and hosting providers.

Google Trust Services officially rolled out server-side support for this in July 2026:
[July 2026 - Google Trust Services Supports ACME dns-account-01 Challenge](https://developers.google.com/public-key-infrastructure/updates/july2026-dns-account-01)

The specification is detailed here:
[draft-ietf-acme-dns-account-challenge](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-acme-dns-account-challenge/)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
* **Subdomain Isolation:** Moving external providers to only validate explicit subdomains (`_acme-challenge.app` and `_acme-challenge.www`), leaving the root `_acme-challenge` empty for `cert-manager`. This is administratively heavy and limits flexibility.
* **HTTP-01 Validation:** Forcing external providers to use HTTP-01, which is not always supported or ideal for our edge routing rules.
* **Centralized Issuance:** Using `cert-manager` as the single source of truth and writing custom automation scripts to push renewed certificates to the Fastly and Kinsta APIs. This defeats the purpose of those platforms' built-in automated TLS management.

**Additional context**
Support for this draft standard would massively simplify TLS automation for any organization adopting a hybrid/multi-CDN edge architecture alongside Kubernetes. Since major CAs like Google Trust Services are already supporting it in production, having client-side support in `cert-manager` would immediately solve a major pain point for complex DNS routing.

## Summary

When using cert-manager with the Venafi TPP in-tree issuer, there is currently 
no way to pass `CASpecificAttributes` from the `Certificate` resource.

This is a blocker for organizations where the Venafi TPP instance requires 
`CASpecificAttributes` (such as `description`) as a mandatory field on 
every certificate request.

---

## Problem

The Venafi WebSDK `/Certificates/Request` endpoint supports a `CASpecificAttributes` 
block:

\```json
{
  "PolicyDN": "XXXXXXX",
  "Subject": "test.comr",
  "Organization": "xxx",
  "OrganizationalUnit": "xxxx",
  "City": "xx",
  "State": "xxxx",
  "Country": "xxxx",
  "CASpecificAttributes": [
    {
      "Name": "description",
      "Value": "this is a test description"
    }
  ],
  "CustomFields": [
  {
      "Name": "label",
      "Values": [
        "xxxxx"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

\```

📄 Venafi API reference:
> https://docs.venafi.com/Docs/currentSDK/TopNav/Content/SDK/AuthSDK/cco-sdka-REST-API-reference.php

Currently, cert-manager only supports injecting `CustomFields` via the annotation 
`venafi.cert-manager.io/custom-fields`. There is no equivalent mechanism 
for `CASpecificAttributes`.

---

## Feature Request

Add support for `CASpecificAttributes` in the `Certificate` resource 
when using the Venafi TPP issuer.

### Option A : New dedicated annotation

\```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: my-app-cert
  namespace: my-namespace
  annotations:
    venafi.cert-manager.io/custom-fields: |
      [
        {
          "name": "my-custom-field",
          "value": "my-value"
        }
      ]
    # Proposed new annotation
    venafi.cert-manager.io/ca-specific-attributes: |
      [
        {
          "name": "description",
          "value": "my certificate description"
        }
      ]
spec:
  secretName: my-app-tls
  commonName: my-app.example.com
  dnsNames:
    - my-app.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: my-venafi-issuer
    kind: Issuer
    group: cert-manager.io
\```

### Option B : Extend existing annotation with a `type` field

\```yaml
venafi.cert-manager.io/custom-fields: |
  [
    {
      "name": "my-custom-field",
      "value": "my-value",
      "type": "CustomField"
    },
    {
      "name": "description",
      "value": "my certificate description",
      "type": "CASpecificAttribute"
    }
  ]
\```

---

## Environment

| Component | Version |
|-----------|---------|
| cert-manager | v1.19 |
| Issuer type | Venafi TPP (in-tree) |

---

## References

- Venafi WebSDK API reference:
  https://docs.venafi.com/Docs/currentSDK/TopNav/Content/SDK/AuthSDK/cco-sdka-REST-API-reference.php
- cert-manager Venafi issuer docs:
  https://cert-manager.io/v1.19-docs/configuration/venafi/

On compatible issuers, acme ARI information should be correctly reported after enabling ARI

body_text:
### What happened?

In `examples/split-editors`, removing the currently focused last editor leaves
the surviving editor unfocused. Typing does nothing until Tab or Shift+Tab is
pressed. The remaining editor should receive focus immediately.

The remove handler truncates `m.inputs` and clamps `m.focus`, but does not call
`Focus()` on the surviving textarea. Its focus flag is still false after the
previous Tab operation. Removing a last editor that is not focused does not
have this problem.

### What happened?

Both HTTP snippets in `tutorials/commands/README.md` (`checkServer` and
`checkSomeUrl`) return the status without closing the response body after a
successful GET. The runnable `tutorials/commands/main.go` already defers
`res.Body.Close()`. Readers copying the README therefore miss the cleanup that
the corresponding source demonstrates.

Expected: close each successful response body before the command finishes.
Actual: a tracking body remains unclosed when either documented command returns.
This is a documentation/example ownership error, not a measured memory-leak claim.

### How can we reproduce this?

Copy either function from the README. In a small harness, replace
`http.DefaultTransport` with a RoundTripper returning a response with status 200
and this body, retaining a pointer to it:

```go
type trackingBody struct{ closed bool }
func (*trackingBody) Read([]byte) (int, error) { return 0, io.EOF }
func (b *trackingBody) Close() error { b.closed = true; return nil }
```

Call `checkServer()` or `checkSomeUrl("https://example.invalid/")()` and inspect
`closed` after return. Both produce status 200 and `closed == false`. Adding
`defer res.Body.Close()` after each successful error check makes it true.
Restore the original transport after the check; no network request is needed.

I verified both snippets with an in-memory transport and an AST comparison
against the README functions. The explicit-close control passed.

### Which version of bubbletea are you using?

Main commit `73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290`.

### Which terminals did you reproduce this with?

Windows Go 1.26.3; a noninteractive HTTP-command harness, no terminal or live
server required.

### Search

- [x] I searched open/closed issues, PRs, discussions and file history.

The existing source-only cleanup in commit `22d15ef` does not update the two
README snippets. Discussion #562 concerns message types, not response cleanup.

**Describe the bug**

When the terminal does not answer Bubble Tea's Unicode-core mode query, the
renderer keeps the WcWidth screen-buffer method. The `tea.Println` path then
counts the inserted text with `ansi.StringWidth`, which uses grapheme-width
semantics. The two calculations disagree for some emoji sequences.

With an eight-column buffer, `🏳️‍🌈aaaaaaa` fits according to the active WcWidth
buffer, but `insertAbove` counts it as wider than the buffer. The renderer
therefore emits one additional newline for the same visual input that the
ASCII control occupies in one line. In a real application this leaves a blank
row or shifts the managed view after `tea.Println` output is inserted.

**Setup**

 - OS [see attachments/environment.txt](attachments/environment.txt)
 - Shell [see attachments/environment.txt](attachments/environment.txt)
 - Terminal Emulator [eight-column PTY; see attachments/environment.txt](attachments/environment.txt)
 - Terminal Multiplexer [none]

The source under test is Bubble Tea v2 at audited revision
`73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290`.

**To Reproduce**

From this report directory, run:

```sh
bash attachments/repro.sh
```

The script builds a small Bubble Tea v2 program and runs it in an eight-column
PTY. It deliberately does not answer `CSI ?2027$p`, then compares an ASCII
control with `🏳️‍🌈aaaaaaa`. Three consecutive runs produced the same result:

```text
PASS case=ascii default-wc insertion newlines=1
FAIL unicode grapheme changed Wc insertion offset: expected=1 actual=2
checked=2 failures=1
```

The complete captured traces and run hashes are in
[attachments/evidence.log](attachments/evidence.log). The terminal-query setup
is recorded in [attachments/environment.txt](attachments/environment.txt).

**Source Code**

The audited revision is
`73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290`, the public Bubble Tea `main`
revision checked for this report on 2026-09-12.

`Program.Println` queues a `printLineMessage` in
[tea.go](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290/tea.go#L1377-L1385).
The normal startup path creates a `cursedRenderer` and asks the terminal for
Unicode-core mode (2027) in
[tea.go](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290/tea.go#L1064-L1074)
and
[tea.go](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290/tea.go#L1118-L1124).
If the terminal does not report that mode, the screen buffer remains on its
default WcWidth method. The method switch itself is visible in
[cursed_renderer.go](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290/cursed_renderer.go#L739-L753).

The mismatch is in `insertAbove`: it obtains the active buffer dimensions at
lines 765–767, splits the queued text into logical lines, and then computes the
extra wrapped-line count with `ansi.StringWidth` at lines 776–783. The
subsequent newline insertion uses that count at line 786:

[cursed_renderer.go](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/73b6d91ac1c3854dd4af046ab5f9e51d3b3b4290/cursed_renderer.go#L756-L786)

The renderer consequently mixes the active buffer's width policy with a
separate grapheme-width measurement. A terminal that successfully enables
Unicode-core mode does not exercise this fallback, which is why the missing
terminal response is part of the reproducer rather than an incidental detail.

**Expected behavior**

The line-count calculation should use the width method of the active screen
buffer. In the fallback case, the Unicode input above should produce the same
single inserted line as the eight-column ASCII control, rather than adding an
extra blank row.

**Screenshots**

No screenshots were captured.

**Additional context**

I searched the existing Bubble Tea issues and did not find a report for this
`tea.Println`/`insertAbove` width-policy mismatch. Issues
[#1736](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/1736),
[#1740](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/1740),
[#1741](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/pull/1741), and
[#1742](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/pull/1742) concern flushing,
first-flush cursor movement, or related renderer sequencing. They do not cover
a stable extra newline caused by a wide grapheme in the WcWidth fallback.

The report artifacts are:

- [repro.sh](attachments/repro.sh)
- [evidence.log](attachments/evidence.log)
- [environment.txt](attachments/environment.txt)
- [attachments.zip](attachments.zip)

body_text:
## Problem

`tea.ClearScreen` (added for https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/236) erases the renderer cell buffer, but it does not re-enter alternate-screen / input / cursor modes. Combined with the unchanged-view skip in `cursedRenderer.flush`, an app cannot recover when something outside the renderer mutates the tty.

Reproduced against v2.0.5 (and the exported API is unchanged through v2.0.9):

1. Program is in the alternate screen with a stable frame.
2. A child (or any other writer) emits `ESC[?1049l`. The physical terminal is now on the primary screen; the renderer still believes its full alt-screen frame is present.
3. The next content change paints only the cell delta (a few bytes). No `1049h`.
4. `tea.ClearScreen` with a byte-identical view writes nothing on a live tick (`flush` returns early because `!starting && viewEquals(lastView, view)`).
5. The next changed frame after ClearScreen redraws text, still without re-entering the alternate screen.

`Program.RestoreTerminal` already proves the repair: `renderer.start()` replays modes from `lastView`, sets `starting = true` so the skip cannot fire, then `flush` emits a full frame. There is no in-loop equivalent that does this without leaving the alternate screen.

This is the same failure class #236 pointed at: a tool writes to the tty, the display is corrupt, and the app needs a forced redraw. ClearScreen never re-acquired modes, so it did not close that case.

## Proposed API

```go
func Repaint() Msg
```

Handled next to `clearScreenMsg`. The renderer, in one locked transaction:

1. `reset()` — drop cell-diff assumptions (fresh `uv.TerminalRenderer`)
2. replay modes from `lastView` (the body of `start()`, extracted so it can run under the existing lock)
3. set `starting = true` so the next flush cannot skip an unchanged view
4. `MoveTo(0, 0)` + `Erase()` — a fresh renderer thinks the screen is blank, so cells that are blank in our frame would otherwise leave stale content in place

A nil `lastView` (very early startup) is a no-op on modes plus erase.

This is not implemented by toggling `View.AltScreen` or writing escapes around the renderer: both leave the cell cache wrong.

`ClearScreen` stays as-is for wiping visual clutter in inline mode. `Repaint` is the recovery operation.

## Tests

- `ClearScreen` + identical alt-screen view does not emit `ESC[?1049h` (the neutralized-fix baseline).
- `Repaint` + identical alt-screen view does re-enter the alternate screen and redraw the content.
- Proof is against renderer output bytes, not `Model.View()`. Send+Quit cannot prove this: `flush(closing=true)` already bypasses the skip.

Happy to send a PR.

2. A child (or any other writer) emits `ESC[?1049l`. The physical terminal is now on the primary screen; the renderer still believes its full alt-screen frame is present.
3. The next content change paints only the cell delta (a few bytes). No `1049h`.
4. `tea.ClearScreen` with a byte-identical view writes nothing on a live tick (`flush` returns early because `!starting && viewEquals(lastView, view)`).
5. The next changed frame after ClearScreen redraws text, still without re-entering the alternate screen.

`Program.RestoreTerminal` already proves the repair: `renderer.start()` replays modes from `lastView`, sets `starting = true` so the skip cannot fire, then `flush` emits a full frame. There is no in-loop equivalent that does this without leaving the alternate screen.

This is the same failure class #236 pointed at: a tool writes to the tty, the display is corrupt, and the app needs a forced redraw. ClearScreen never re-acquired modes, so it did not close that case.

## Proposed API

```go
func Repaint() Msg
```

Handled next to `clearScreenMsg`. The renderer, in one locked transaction:

1. `reset()` — drop cell-diff assumptions (fresh `uv.TerminalRenderer`)
2. replay modes from `lastView` (the body of `start()`, extracted so it can run under the existing lock)
3. set `starting = true` so the next flush cannot skip an unchanged view
4. `MoveTo(0, 0)` + `Erase()` — a fresh renderer thinks the screen is blank, so cells that are blank in our frame would otherwise leave stale content in place

A nil `lastView` (very early startup) is a no-op on modes plus erase.

This is not implemented by toggling `View.AltScreen` or writing escapes around the renderer: both leave the cell cache wrong.

`ClearScreen` stays as-is for wiping visual clutter in inline mode. `Repaint` is the recovery operation.

## Tests

- `ClearScreen` + identical alt-screen view does not emit `ESC[?1049h` (the neutralized-fix baseline).
- `Repaint` + identical alt-screen view does re-enter the alternate screen and redraw the content.
- Proof is against renderer output bytes, not `Model.View()`. Send+Quit cannot prove this: `flush(closing=true)` already bypasses the skip.

Happy to send a PR.

**Describe the bug**

In inline mode, one `tea.Println` containing more rows than the terminal can accommodate above the managed View removes the already-rendered View. The View stays byte-for-byte identical throughout the reproduction.

This occurs **after the initial frame is visibly rendered**, with no resize, model switch, streaming, raw terminal output, or clear-screen operation. All printed lines are short ASCII strings, so this is not a wrapping or wide-grapheme case.

I reproduced it with the latest release, `charm.land/bubbletea/v2 v2.0.10`, and with the renderer/Program source from current `main` (`ff51ba4c51f85875761b15a64f9ab9aa0eaa9fa1`). The renderer file on that commit is identical to v2.0.10; the additional main-branch change concerns shutdown signal handling.

**Setup**

- OS: macOS 26.5.1, arm64
- Go: go1.26.6 darwin/arm64
- Reproduction environment: a local controlling PTY at **40 columns × 10 rows**, whose output is replayed in pyte 0.8.2 for screen/history assertions
- Environment: `TERM=xterm-256color`, `TERM_PROGRAM=Apple_Terminal`, `NO_COLOR=1`. The `TERM_PROGRAM` value is an explicit harness setting, not a claim that the test ran in the Apple Terminal GUI.
- Shell: the harness launches the compiled binary directly; no shell is involved
- SSH / terminal multiplexer: none
- Also observed with renderer-level screen assertions using `github.com/charmbracelet/x/vt`

**To Reproduce**

1. Put the source below in `main.go` in a new directory and run:

   ```sh
   go mod init bubbletea-inline-repro
   go get charm.land/bubbletea/v2@v2.0.10
   go run .
   ```

2. Use a 40×10 terminal, or a terminal substantially shorter than the 80 printed rows.
3. Wait until `COMPOSER`, `STATUS`, and the key hint are visible. This matters: the example does not print from `Init`, and the first View has already been painted.
4. Press `p` once.
5. Observe the screen **before pressing `q`**, since shutdown may repaint the View.

**Source Code**

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"

	tea "charm.land/bubbletea/v2"
)

type model struct{}

func (model) Init() tea.Cmd { return nil }

func (m model) Update(message tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
	if key, ok := message.(tea.KeyPressMsg); ok {
		switch key.String() {
		case "p":
			lines := make([]string, 80)
			for i := range lines {
				lines[i] = fmt.Sprintf("ROW-%03d", i)
			}
			return m, tea.Println(strings.Join(lines, "\n"))
		case "q", "ctrl+c":
			return m, tea.Quit
		}
	}
	return m, nil
}

func (model) View() tea.View {
	view := tea.NewView("COMPOSER\nSTATUS\np: print history | q: quit")
	view.Cursor = tea.NewCursor(0, 0)
	return view
}

func main() {
	if _, err := tea.NewProgram(model{}).Run(); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

**Expected behavior**

- `ROW-000` through `ROW-079` enter native history exactly once and in order.
- The three-line managed View remains visible beneath that output.
- The visible cursor is restored to the View's requested position.
- Neither another keypress nor a changed View/resize/Quit should be required to repair the screen.

**Actual screen**

Captured after `p`, before any further input or Quit (trailing spaces omitted):

```text
ROW-071
ROW-072
ROW-073
ROW-074
ROW-075
ROW-076
ROW-077
ROW-078
ROW-079

```

`COMPOSER`, `STATUS`, and the key hint are absent. The terminal cursor is at `(0,9)` instead of on the managed View. In this single-print minimal example, all 80 numbered rows are still present and ordered in screen + history; the demonstrated failure is the lost managed View/cursor, not lost message data.

| Source under test | Initial View observed before `p` | All 80 rows ordered and unique | Managed controls visible after print |
|---|---|---|---|
| Official v2.0.10 | yes | yes | no |
| Current main renderer/Program source (`ff51ba4c51f85`) | yes | yes | no |
| Local renderer fix | yes | yes | yes |

**Additional context / likely cause**

In [`insertAbove`](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/blob/ff51ba4c51f85875761b15a64f9ab9aa0eaa9fa1/cursed_renderer.go), the payload row count is reserved below the managed frame using newlines, followed by `CursorUp(offset + h - 1)` and `InsertLine(offset)`. With an 80-row payload on a 10-row terminal containing a 3-row View, the reservation exceeds the 7 available rows and displaces the managed content. The final internal cursor reset does not repaint it; the equal-View fast path can then skip the necessary restoration.

I searched open and closed issues and PRs. These are related, but their reproducers concern different conditions:

- #1736 / #1741: a changed View has not yet been flushed. Here the View was already painted and never changes height/content.
- #1740 / #1766: printing before the first flush. Here `p` is sent only after the complete first frame is visible.
- #1613 / #1678: model-switching overwrite, previously fixed. There is no model switch here.
- #1666: raw output following a native clear/reset. This example uses neither raw output nor a clear operation.
- #959: historical width truncation; the lines here are only 7 columns wide.

I did not find a report covering this already-flushed, fixed-geometry, oversized-insertion case. If you prefer tracking it under an existing issue, I am happy to consolidate the reproduction there.

We have a local fix that keeps insertion inside the renderer, uses execution-time geometry, avoids oversized blank-row reservations, and restores the managed frame/cursor before returning. **We would be happy to submit a focused PR with automated regression tests**, including the no-free-rows/full-height case. We can coordinate with #1741 rather than duplicating its pending-frame-flush work. No new public printing API is required by the local approach.

body_text:
`handleSignals` (tea.go:665-706) forwards the first SIGINT/SIGTERM as a quit/interrupt message and then `return`s. The deferred `signal.Stop(sig)` (tea.go:680) releases Go's subscription for the whole `shutdown()` window (tea.go:1285-1310) — which includes waiting on the channel handlers and the read loop, plus the renderer's final flush and close, i.e. real I/O time.

So: first SIGTERM starts a graceful quit; a second SIGTERM or SIGINT arriving before shutdown completes takes the runtime's default path — Go re-raises it via `dieFromSignal`, so the process dies by that signal just as it would under `SIG_DFL` (unless the signal was inherited ignored). `restoreTerminalState()` (tty.go:34) never runs and the tty is left in raw mode.

Repro (needs a pty): a program whose output writer sleeps ~1.5s per `Write` to widen the shutdown window, run under a pseudo-terminal, then:

    kill -TERM $pid; sleep 0.3; kill -TERM $pid; wait $pid

Observed: the process dies by the signal (`Terminated: 15`), `Run` never returns, and `stty -a` afterwards shows `lflags: -icanon -isig -iexten -echo` — raw mode left behind for the user's shell. With a single SIGTERM the same program exits 0 with `icanon`/`echo` restored.

Expected: a second signal during shutdown is either ignored or still leads to a graceful exit with the terminal restored.

The obvious directions are (a) keep the handler registered until the program context is cancelled so subsequent signals during shutdown are caught and ignored, or (b) on a second signal, restore the terminal before exiting. (a) is a very small change but means a wedged shutdown can no longer be force-killed by repeated SIGTERM (SIGKILL still works); (b) preserves force-quit semantics at the cost of a more involved exit path. Happy to PR whichever you prefer — let me know.

body_text:
`Run` enters raw mode inside `initTerminal` (tea.go:1064 -> `initInput` -> `term.MakeRaw`, tty_unix.go:19; on Windows tty_windows.go:19), but several error returns after that point go back to the caller without restoring the terminal state:

- tea.go:1064-1066 — `initTerminal` itself failing. On unix there's no error path after `MakeRaw` succeeds, but on Windows the input is made raw *before* the output console-mode setup, so an output-setup failure returns with input left raw.
- tea.go:1072-1075 — `term.GetSize` on the output tty failing.
- tea.go:1129-1131 — `initInputReader` failing (e.g. the cancelreader can't allocate its kqueue/pipe fds).

So any error between "raw mode entered" and "event loop started" returns without `restoreTerminalState` running.

Repro (needs a pty): lower `RLIMIT_NOFILE` to the current number of open fds so `uv.NewCancelReader` fails, run a trivial quit-immediately program under `script`, and inspect stdin termios after `Run` returns.

Observed: `Run` returns `bubbletea: could not create cancelable reader: pipe: too many open files`, and `TIOCGETA` on stdin afterwards shows `ICANON=false ECHO=false` — the user's shell is left in raw mode.

Expected: `Run` returns the error *and* restores the terminal (`ICANON`/`ECHO` set again). The fix is presumably just calling `restoreTerminalState` on these error paths — happy to PR it if that sounds right.

body_text:
When stdin isn't a TTY, `Run` opens the controlling terminal via `OpenTTY` and keeps it as `p.input` (tea.go:1039-1044; `uv.OpenTTY` opens `/dev/tty` once `O_RDWR`, tty_unix.go:15-21 in ultraviolet). Nothing ever closes that file — there's no `p.input.Close()` anywhere, the cancelreader doesn't own the fd, and `restoreInput` (tty.go:41) only restores termios.

So each `Run` with non-TTY stdin leaks one fd until Go's GC finalizer happens to reclaim the `*os.File`. Processes that run many programs in-process — test harnesses, servers embedding TUIs, repeated `Run` loops — accumulate fds, and under fd pressure or with GC disabled this can exhaust the limit.

Repro: 50 immediate-quit `Run`s with stdin redirected from `/dev/null`, under a controlling tty, counting `/dev/fd` before and after. With `GOGC=off`: `before=5 after=58` — about one fd per `Run`. With GC on the count oscillates instead (finalizers reclaim the files eventually), so it's easy to miss, but it's still a real leak — just lazily reclaimed.

On Windows it leaks a bit more: `openTTY` there opens `CONIN$` and `CONOUT$` as separate files, and the output handle is discarded at the call site, so both handles are lost.

Expected: fd count stable across N `Run`s — the files `Run` opens get closed when it returns, on success and on error paths. Happy to PR a fix if you'd like one.

body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

A key press reaches the terminal only on the renderer's next frame tick. Every keystroke therefore waits up to one frame period (16.7 ms at the default 60 fps) before its echo is written. On a real program (a coding-agent TUI at 120×40 with a long transcript) we measured **13.1 ms median keystroke-to-echo** (p95 15.6 ms) through a pseudo-terminal. That is noticeably laggy next to shells and editors, which echo in about 1 ms.

Two things contribute:

1. **Frame-tick latency.** `Program.eventLoop` runs `Update` and `View` for the key at once, but the renderer writes only on `p.ticker`. `WithFPS(120)` halves the wait (we measured 5.6 ms) but doesn't remove it, and doubles idle wake-ups.
2. **Full-screen diff per frame.** `cursedRenderer.flush` clears `cellbuf` and redraws the whole view, which marks every line as touched. The terminal renderer then re-diffs every line, even when a keystroke changed one. This is the same cost #1724 describes for scrolling.

Reproduction: at `WithFPS(1)`, type a key just after a frame has flushed. Its frame appears only at the next tick, about 1 s later. The test in the PR below does exactly this and fails on `main` with "the key's frame took 999.9ms".

**Describe the solution you'd like**

1. After `Update`/`View` for **user input** (key, paste, mouse messages), signal the renderer goroutine to flush at once instead of waiting for the tick. Everything else (streaming output, timers, `Send`) stays rate-limited by the ticker, so throughput and idle behaviour don't change.
2. Draw the frame into a scratch buffer and copy and mark as touched **only the lines that changed**. Above a small number of changed lines (8), mark everything as today.

With both changes, the same program measured **1.3 ms median** (p95 2.7 ms), and bytes written per keystroke were unchanged. In isolation, (2) cuts one keystroke frame at 120×40 from 477.7 µs to 348.6 µs (benchmark included).

I have both as small, separate PRs with tests (linked below), opened as drafts so you can decide whether you want them.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- `WithFPS(120)`: halves the latency, doubles idle ticks.
- `WithoutRenderer()` plus an application-side renderer: duplicates the renderer, and every app has to do it.
- Patching Bubble Tea downstream: a `replace` breaks `go install …@latest` for the application, so we would rather fix it here.

**Additional context**

While testing on `main` I noticed that since ultraviolet `6b8d4baf` (the bump after v2.0.10), a frame re-sends **unchanged lines that contain wide characters** on every flush. For example, with `emoji 🎉 here` on line 2, typing on line 3 writes `\x1b[?7l…\x1b[Kemoji 🎉 here\x1b[?7h…` each frame, where v2.0.10 with ultraviolet `f5a850f9` wrote `\rX`. The changed-lines PR happens to avoid it, but it is probably worth its own look in ultraviolet.

Related: #1724 (scroll frame cost), #1796 and #1832 (ticker idling).
